report.releaseDate: 22 Oct 2026 (GR8_TECH "Operator Lens: Brazil"); underlying event: MP 1.394/2026 of 25 Sep 2026
report.currency: BRL (R$) primary; ~USD alongside at USD/BRL 5.10. Tables in R$ billions unless stated.
report.verdict: Brazil has gone from the world's newest large regulated online market (SPA-reported GGR of R$36.96bn (~$7.25bn) in 2025, 84 licensees and 193 brands by mid-2026) to a nationwide prohibition in 21 months: Provisional Measure 1.394/2026 barred deposits from 25 Sep 2026, took every site offline on 6 Oct and extinguished all authorisations on 25 Oct with no refund of the R$30m (~$5.9m) licence fees. The ban's permanence now rests on a Congress that had not even seated the MP committee as of 4 Nov, an STF rapporteur (Fux) who has publicly said he thinks bets should be banned, and a president re-elected on 25 Oct who is campaigning for the prohibition to hold. For B2Tech there is no lawful addressable market today; this is a binary watch-list jurisdiction until at least Q1 2027.

summary: **The market has been prohibited, not reformed.** MP 1.394/2026 (DOU Extra A, 25 Sep 2026) bans the exploitation, offer, intermediation and advertising of fixed-odds lotteries — sports betting and online games — in physical and virtual environments, explicitly including offshore operators targeting people in Brazil and state/DF concessions. Only other lottery modalities (Caixa's federal lotteries) are carved out.

**The shutdown was executed in 30 days.** New deposits were barred from 25 Sep; voluntary withdrawals closed 23:59 on 5 Oct; sites and apps (including app-store listings) went dark on 6 Oct; operators reported residual balances by CPF to banks on 6–8 Oct; banks refunded 9–14 Oct; Caixa Econômica Federal took over unresolved refunds from 15 Oct; all authorisations were extinguished on 25 Oct 'for reasons of public interest' with no refund of outorgas and no indemnity.

**Pre-ban, Brazil was a ~R$40bn-a-year GGR market.** The SPA's Panorama Periódico reports FY2025 GGR of R$36,959,783,380 (~$7.25bn): R$17.4bn (~$3.41bn) in H1 and an implied R$19.56bn (~$3.84bn) in H2 (+12.4% HoH). H1-2026 GGR was R$20.07bn (~$3.94bn) on SPA data released via access-to-information requests (+15.3% YoY), or R$20.28bn (~$3.98bn, +6.2%) on brmkt.co's later SIGAP extraction, which also restates FY2025 to R$40.69bn (~$7.98bn). We anchor on the regulator's published figures and flag the ~R$3.7bn FY2025 gap.

**Momentum was already fading into the ban.** Monthly GGR fell from R$4.29bn (~$0.84bn) in Jan-2026 to R$3.50bn (~$0.69bn) in June (-18.5%); deposits fell 30% over the same window (R$18.65bn → R$13.06bn) and 12.4% YoY for the half (R$88.48bn (~$17.35bn) vs R$100.99bn). Deposits falling faster than GGR lifted implied hold from 18.9% to 22.9% — consistent with a casino-heavy mix and the statutory ban on sign-up bonuses.

**The market is effectively 100% online.** All regulated fixed-odds revenue runs through .bet.br digital platforms; retail fixed-odds was negligible and Caixa's lottery network sits outside this regime (and outside the ban). Mobile accounted for ~63% of Brazilian web traffic in Sep 2026 (GR8_TECH).

**Participation was mass-market.** 17.7m unique CPFs bet in H1-2025, 25.2m across FY2025 (SPA) and 30.4m in H1-2026 (BNLData). Implied annual GGR per bettor was R$1,467 (~$288) in 2025; 68.5% of H1-2026 bettors were male and roughly four in ten were under 30; 44.4% used a single operator and 27.8% used four or more (Q1-2026).

**Licensing regime (Law 14.790/2023, SPA/MF) — now void.** Federal authorisation cost R$30m (~$5.9m) for up to three brands over five years; 78 companies/182 brands were live in mid-2025, 79 companies at Dec-2025 and 84 companies/193 brands by H1-2026. Roughly R$2.5bn (~$0.49bn) of outorgas has been rendered worthless with no compensation; pending applications were voided and new grants are barred.

**Tax regime — base was GGR.** Operators paid a 12% statutory contribution on GGR (R$4.53bn (~$0.89bn) in 2025; R$2.49bn (~$0.49bn) in H1-2026, +16%), a monthly supervision fee (R$95.5m (~$18.7m) in 2025) and ordinary corporate taxes; bettors paid 15% income tax on net prizes. Total federal collection from the sector was R$9.95bn (~$1.95bn) in 2025 (~27% of GGR) and R$7.3bn (~$1.43bn) in H1-2026 (+92% YoY, secondary source).

**The Treasury is knowingly forgoing revenue.** The MP's own exposição de motivos books revenue losses of R$1.541bn (~$0.30bn) in 2026, R$5.150bn (~$1.01bn) in 2027 and R$5.330bn (~$1.05bn) in 2028, plus R$268.8m (~$52.7m) of supervision-fee losses over three years — i.e., the government is budgeting for prohibition to persist through 2028.

**Payments have been weaponised.** Banks, payment institutions and Pix participants are barred from processing betting transactions; the Central Bank must build an electronic system to reject and return betting-related instant payments. Pre-ban, SPA rules already restricted funding to Pix/TED/debit from bettor-named accounts (no credit cards, no crypto), and an STF injunction (Fux, 13 Nov 2024) barred Bolsa Família/BPC funds.

**Advertising and sponsorship are fully prohibited.** All marketing and sponsorship had to be removed by 5 Oct 2026; non-compliant advertising is 'abusive' under the Consumer Code; internet platforms and app stores must proactively block betting content, with fines of up to 10% of Brazilian group revenue or R$10–1,000 (~$2–196) per registered user capped at R$50m (~$9.8m). Every Série A club had a master sponsor in 2025, mostly bets; ~US$200m of football sponsorship is at risk and Flamengo alone cited ~R$45m (~$8.8m) of R$290m (~$57m) revenue.

**Enforcement is being scaled up, not down.** In the two weeks to 9 Oct authorities submitted 16,627 gambling sites for blocking and 3,691 social/messaging profiles for removal, versus >25,000 sites blocked in all of 2025. Anatel distributes blocking orders to ISPs, CGI.br handles .br domains, and a Casa Civil-chaired Interinstitutional Committee coordinates PF, Receita Federal and Coaf.

**The illegal market was already large.** Research cited by GR8_TECH found three in four Brazilian bettors used unauthorised sites at least once in 2025; the SPA logged 132 enforcement proceedings against licensees in 2025 (80 heading to penalties) and >217k self-exclusions on its centralised platform.

**Congress has not moved.** The MP's joint committee was designated on 30 Sep but remained 'awaiting installation' with no chair or rapporteur on 4 Nov; 99 amendments (5 withdrawn) were filed by 13 Oct; the urgency regime locks the floor agenda from 9 Nov; the initial validity window ends 23 Nov 2026, extendable 60 days (nominally ~23 Jan 2027, with the recess likely pushing the practical deadline into Feb 2027). If it lapses unconverted the prohibition falls — but licences have already been extinguished.

**The STF is the other gate — and the rapporteur leans pro-ban.** ADI 8.027 (ANJL) seeks suspension of the MP; Justice Fux held a 10-hour public hearing with 28 entities on 3 Nov 2026, at which the AGU argued the regulated model had failed, the Health Minister cited a 15x higher suicide risk among e-bettors, clubs and the CBF asked for a gradual transition, and Fux said his perception is that online bets should be banned. No ruling has been issued.

**Politics cut against re-opening.** The MP was issued nine days before the first round, when Quaest had Flávio Bolsonaro at 42%; Lula won the 25 Oct run-off with 51.79% of valid votes and on 3 Nov urged civil society to 'pressure' for the ban to stay. The opposition's line — distinguishing online casinos from sports betting — is the only visible compromise space. Senate e-Cidadania polling ran ~199k for vs 70.6k against (28 Sep).

**Read-through for B2Tech: no lawful route exists today.** Brazil has demonstrated regulatory expropriation without compensation; any grey-market play faces Pix rejection, CDC liability, platform de-listing and PF/Coaf exposure. Treat Brazil as a scenario-driven watch-list market with a binary outcome by Q1 2027; redeploy Portuguese-language product and LatAm capacity elsewhere, and only re-engage if Congress rebuilds a (likely sports-only, ad-restricted) regime with fresh licensing.

**Data confidence is MEDIUM.** FY2025 and H1-2025 figures are regulator-published; H1-2026 figures come from SPA data released via LAI and a consultancy's SIGAP extraction that disagree by 1%; no GGR split by sports vs casino is published; market shares are not disclosed by the SPA.

segments.name: Online sports betting & iGaming (regulated fixed-odds market, Jan-2025 to Sep-2026)
segments.headline: A ~R$40bn annualised GGR market with 30m bettors was growing double-digit on the regulator's series but decelerating month by month before it was switched off.
narrative: The regulated market opened on 1 January 2025 under Law 14.790/2023, with the Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas (SPA) of the Finance Ministry as licensor and supervisor and operators reporting daily through the SIGAP system. The SPA's Panorama Periódico for 2025 puts first-year GGR at R$36,959,783,380 (~$7.25bn): R$17.4bn (~$3.41bn) in H1 and an implied R$19.56bn (~$3.84bn) in H2, a 12.4% half-on-half step-up. GGR here is stakes less prizes paid, gross of the 12% levy and of corporate tax; the SPA does not publish a sports-versus-casino split, so product mix must be inferred from survey data.

For 2026 the regulator has not released a comparable mid-year Panorama; the two available series disagree. SPA data obtained under access-to-information law and published by BNLData show H1-2026 GGR of R$20.07bn (~$3.94bn), +15.3% on the SPA's own H1-2025 figure. brmkt.co's extraction of SIGAP data dated 8 Sep 2026 shows R$20.28bn (~$3.98bn), +6.2% against a restated R$19.09bn for H1-2025, and restates FY2025 to R$40.69bn (~$7.98bn). The ~R$3.7bn FY2025 gap most plausibly reflects late or corrected operator filings after the January Panorama was cut; we anchor on the regulator's published numbers and treat the consultancy series as the better guide to trend.

The trend into the ban was negative. Monthly GGR fell from R$4.29bn (~$0.84bn) in January 2026 to R$3.50bn (~$0.69bn) in June, an 18.5% decline, while deposits dropped 30% from R$18.65bn (~$3.66bn) to R$13.06bn (~$2.56bn). Half-year deposits of R$88.48bn (~$17.35bn) were 12.4% below the R$100.99bn (~$19.8bn) of H1-2025 even as GGR rose, lifting implied hold from 18.9% to 22.9%. A rising hold on falling deposits is the signature of a casino-weighted mix and of the statutory prohibition on sign-up bonuses, which removed the main promotional lever that depresses hold in sportsbook-led markets. Average monthly run-rate in H1-2026 was R$3.38bn (~$0.66bn) of GGR on R$14.7bn (~$2.9bn) of deposits.

Participation was mass-market and young. 17.7 million unique CPFs bet in H1-2025, 25.2 million across 2025 (SPA) and 30.4 million in H1-2026 (BNLData; a different extraction, so not strictly comparable). Implied GGR per bettor was R$1,467 (~$288) for 2025 and R$660 (~$129) for H1-2026. In Q1-2026, 44.4% of bettors used a single operator and 27.8% used four or more; 68.5% of H1-2026 bettors were men and roughly four in ten were under 30. On GR8_TECH's survey work, traditional sports draw 70% of bettors and esports 40%, with football central but basketball, volleyball and MMA material; on the casino side slots take 50% of preferences, crash and instant games 25% and live dealer 24%, with fortune-themed slots (the 'tigrinho' Lula cited when signing the MP), Aviator, Mines and Plinko the recognisable favourites. Mobile accounted for roughly 63% of Brazilian web traffic in September 2026.

The regulated market never displaced the unregulated one. Research cited in the GR8_TECH report found three in four Brazilian bettors used unauthorised sites at least once in 2025, despite more than 25,000 illegal domains being blocked by the SPA/Anatel during the year. That leakage — alongside SPA data showing 132 enforcement proceedings against licensees — was used by the government to argue that the control mechanisms of Law 14.790 were insufficient, and it is the core of the industry's counter-argument that prohibition simply hands the whole R$40bn to the black market.

For an operator the commercial conclusion is stark: the legal addressable market is zero from 6 October 2026, and the payment, advertising and platform provisions of the MP are designed to make offshore service of Brazilian customers both operationally difficult and legally hazardous. The demand that produced R$20bn of GGR in a half-year has not disappeared; it has been pushed to crypto-funded and intermediated-Pix offshore sites. B2Tech should not route product into Brazil in any form while the MP is in force.

segments.name: Licensing & tax regime — and its extinction under MP 1.394/2026
segments.headline: A R$30m, five-year, 12%-of-GGR regime was expropriated without compensation; the Treasury has booked a R$5bn-a-year revenue loss to do it.
narrative: Fixed-odds betting was legalised by Law 13.756/2018 and given an operating framework by Law 14.790/2023, which the MP now amends. Under that framework a federal authorisation from the SPA cost R$30m (~$5.9m), covered up to three brands and ran for five years; operators had to be Brazilian-incorporated, use .bet.br domains, report through SIGAP, pay a monthly supervision fee and comply with SPA ordinances on responsible gambling, advertising and payments (no sign-up bonuses, no credit-card or crypto funding). By mid-2025 78 companies and 182 brands were live, rising to 79 companies at December 2025 and 84 companies with 193 brands by H1-2026 — roughly R$2.5bn (~$0.49bn) of outorga capital in aggregate.

The tax base was GGR. Operators paid a 12% statutory contribution earmarked for social security, sport, health, education, tourism and public security (R$4.53bn (~$0.89bn) in 2025; R$2.49bn (~$0.49bn) in H1-2026), the supervision fee (R$95.5m (~$18.7m) in 2025) and ordinary IRPJ/CSLL/PIS/COFINS/ISS, while bettors paid 15% income tax on net prizes. Total federal collection attributed to the sector was R$9.95bn (~$1.95bn) in 2025, about 27% of GGR, and R$7.3bn (~$1.43bn) in H1-2026 on a secondary tally — a near-doubling that suggests corporate-tax instalments and prize-tax withholding were catching up with the GGR base. An attempt in 2025 to lift the GGR levy from 12% to 18% did not become law [from prior knowledge; not re-verified in this cycle].

MP 1.394/2026 does not alter rates; it abolishes the activity. Article-level provisions reported by Agência Senado and the Finance Ministry prohibit exploitation, offer, intermediation and advertising of fixed-odds lotteries nationwide, including by foreign-domiciled agents serving people in Brazil and under state/DF concessions; bar new deposits from 25 Sep; require platforms to go offline (including app stores) from 6 Oct; void open bets unsettled ten days after publication with full stake refunds; and extinguish all existing authorisations 30 days after publication (25 Oct) 'for reasons of public interest', expressly denying refund of outorgas or any indemnity. Pending applications are voided and new concessions, permits or authorisations are barred. Non-compliance with the refund mechanics carries a daily fine of R$200,000 (~$39k).

Operators' obligations do not die with the licence. Regulatory, tax, financial, AML/CFT, responsible-gambling and sports-integrity duties for the authorised period remain enforceable; bettor, bet, payment and prize records must be retained for at least five years; and operators must transmit to the SPA via SIGAP full data on users, bets, deposits, withdrawals, prizes, residual balances, refunds and revenues earned while licensed. In other words the SPA remains the counterparty for audits and penalties even though it no longer licenses anything.

The exposição de motivos quantifies the cost the government is prepared to bear: R$1.541bn (~$0.30bn) of lost revenue in 2026, R$5.150bn (~$1.01bn) in 2027 and R$5.330bn (~$1.05bn) in 2028, plus R$38.4m (~$7.5m) of supervision-fee losses in Sep–Dec 2026 and R$115.2m (~$22.6m) in each of the following two years. The 2027–28 figures sit well below the R$9.95bn actually collected in 2025, which indicates the Treasury's counterfactual mostly counts the 12% levy and the prize tax rather than the full corporate-tax wedge — or that it was already modelling a shrinking market. Either way, the fiscal argument that the industry relied on has been consciously discounted by the Executive, and the stated justification is public health, household indebtedness (net transfers from families to platforms in 2025 put at 'tens of billions of reais') and links to organised crime.

For B2Tech the lesson is about sovereign-regulatory risk pricing rather than tax arithmetic. Brazil has shown that a five-year authorisation can be cancelled in 30 days by provisional measure with no compensation, and that an ordinary-law regime can be overridden without Congress voting first. Any future re-entry should avoid outorga-heavy, front-loaded structures, favour asset-light B2B exposure, and treat the constitutional litigation over 'relevance and urgency' and acquired rights (ADI 8.027) as the test case for whether licence investments in Brazil are ever recoverable.

segments.name: Legislative, judicial & political path (Congress, STF, Planalto)
segments.headline: Three gates — a dormant Congress committee, an STF rapporteur signalling support for the ban, and a re-elected president campaigning to keep it — all currently point to prohibition holding.
narrative: A provisional measure has the force of law from publication but must be converted by both houses within 60 days, extendable once by 60. The Congress calendar sets deliberation from 25 Sep to 23 Nov 2026, with a possible extension to roughly 23 Jan 2027; because the constitutional count is suspended during the December–February recess, the practical outer deadline could slip into February 2027. From 9 Nov the MP enters the urgency regime and locks the floor agenda of whichever house holds it. Before any floor vote a joint committee must issue an opinion; that committee was designated on 30 Sep and its membership published on 1 Oct, but as of 4 Nov it was still 'awaiting installation' with no president, no rapporteur and no meetings scheduled. Ninety-nine amendments were filed by the extended 13 Oct deadline (five later withdrawn), and the Pariente Advisory read — that whatever regime Brazil ends up with will be written in that committee rather than in the original text — is the right frame.

If Congress neither converts nor rejects, the MP lapses and the Law 14.790 regime technically revives, but by then every authorisation has already been extinguished, outorgas forfeited and sites taken down; Congress would normally issue a legislative decree to regulate relations formed while the MP was in force, and absent that the acts stand. A lapse therefore does not restore the market — it creates a licensing vacuum in which the SPA would have to run a new authorisation round under whatever rules survive. Rejection on the floor, by contrast, would be a direct political defeat for a president who has just been re-elected, which is why the committee's inertia is better read as the Congress waiting for the STF and for the post-election realignment than as resistance.

The judicial track runs through ADI 8.027, filed by the operators' association ANJL, which asks the STF to suspend the MP immediately and ultimately to declare it unconstitutional while affirming the constitutionality of the laws that regulated betting. The rapporteur is Justice Luiz Fux, who had already signalled the Court would not act before the election and who, on 13 Nov 2024, granted the injunction in ADIs 7.721/7.723 barring the use of Bolsa Família and BPC benefits for betting and any advertising aimed at children. At the AGU's request he convened a public hearing on 3 Nov 2026: 28 entities and 34 speakers over roughly ten hours, opened by ten football clubs. The AGU argued the prior regulation had proved insufficient to protect health, dignity and family finances; the Health Minister cited a 15-times higher suicide risk among electronic bettors; the CBF and clubs quantified sponsorship losses (Flamengo: ~R$45m (~$8.8m) of R$290m (~$57m) revenue) and asked for a gradual transition and respect for contracts signed under the regulated regime; the industry warned of job losses, match-fixing and black-market growth. Fux closed by saying his own perception is that online bets should be banned in Brazil. No injunction has been granted and no judgment date has been set.

The political context explains both the timing and the durability of the measure. Lula signed the MP in São Paulo on 25 Sep, nine days before the first round, after a 21 Sep Quaest poll put Flávio Bolsonaro at 42%; the ban joined a Bolsa Família increase and a new Desenrola debt programme as late-campaign measures. Lula won the 25 Oct run-off with 51.79% of valid votes and, on the morning of the STF hearing, posted that civil society 'cannot allow the continuation of the bets' and that it was time to pressure. Senate e-Cidadania polling ran roughly 199,000 in favour versus 70,600 against within three days of publication. The opposition's critique has centred on the use of a provisional measure rather than on the merits, and Flávio Bolsonaro's own line distinguished online casinos from sports betting — the clearest marker of where a legislative compromise might land. The direction of travel was visible earlier in 2026: prediction-market platform Polymarket has been blocked in Brazil since April, even as it handled ~US$180m of wagers on the Brazilian election from abroad.

For an operator weighing scenarios, the probabilities are not symmetric. Conversion into law (possibly with amendments on club contracts, refund mechanics and enforcement) or a lapse followed by a replacement government bill both leave prohibition in place through 2027. A committee rewrite that re-creates a narrower regulated regime — sports-only, online casino banned, advertising and sponsorship curbed, deposit limits — is plausible but would need new licensing and could not be operational before late 2027 at the earliest. A judicial suspension by the rapporteur looks the least likely of the three paths after 3 Nov.

segments.name: Payments, enforcement & responsible gambling
segments.headline: Pix — the rail that made Brazil scale — is now the primary enforcement instrument, backed by platform liability and a cross-agency blocking machine.
narrative: Brazil's online betting boom was a Pix phenomenon: instant, free, universal account-to-account payments let 30 million CPFs deposit R$88.48bn (~$17.35bn) in six months, about R$14.7bn (~$2.9bn) a month. The SPA's pre-ban payment rules already confined funding to Pix, TED and debit from accounts in the bettor's own name, prohibited credit cards and crypto, and required segregated transactional accounts at Brazilian institutions. The STF added a welfare firewall in November 2024 when Justice Fux ordered the government to stop Bolsa Família and BPC funds being used for bets. Those design choices are what now make the shutdown enforceable: every regulated flow ran through identifiable Brazilian accounts.

The MP turns the rail against the activity. Banks, payment institutions and all participants in payment arrangements — explicitly including instant-payment schemes — are prohibited from processing or enabling transactions destined for fixed-odds betting, with the sole exception of flows needed to wind down operations and refund players. The Central Bank is directed to build an electronic communication system that lets institutions reject betting-related transfers in real time and return funds interbank. Refunds of unclaimed balances were pushed through the banks between 9 and 14 Oct, with Caixa Econômica Federal acting as refund-of-last-resort from 15 Oct under Finance Ministry supervision. The practical gap — which GR8_TECH flags — is that offshore operators collect through intermediated Pix (gateways, nominee accounts) and crypto on-ramps that do not carry a betting identifier; expect the BCB system and Coaf data-sharing to be aimed at exactly those intermediaries, and expect financial institutions to over-comply.

Blocking and content enforcement have been institutionalised rather than left to the SPA. The Finance and Justice ministries may order blocking or redirection of sites still offering bets; Anatel receives and distributes the orders to ISPs and other intermediaries, and CGI.br handles .br domain names. A Casa Civil-coordinated Interinstitutional Committee is created to run prevention, supervision and repression, with the Federal Police, Receita Federal and Coaf required to share data, and states are expected to cooperate. Internet application providers must proactively prevent and remove content that promotes or facilitates access to bets — including third-party content — and app stores and operating systems must block prohibited products; sanctions run from warnings to fines of up to 10% of the economic group's Brazilian revenue (or R$10–1,000 (~$2–196) per registered user, capped at R$50m (~$9.8m)), daily fines and suspension. Output in the first fortnight — 16,627 sites submitted for blocking and 3,691 social-media and messaging profiles or channels flagged for removal between 25 Sep and 9 Oct — already approaches two-thirds of the >25,000 domains blocked in the whole of 2025.

On the responsible-gambling side the regulated regime had built real infrastructure in 18 months: a centralised SPA self-exclusion platform with more than 217,000 exclusions by end-2025, mandatory self-limits and risk-behaviour monitoring, a consumer-education course run with the national consumer secretariat, a ban on sign-up bonuses and on advertising aimed at minors, and 132 supervisory proceedings against licensees in 2025 of which 80 were heading to penalties. The government's position at the STF was that none of this sufficed against household indebtedness and mental-health harms; the industry's position is that the ban dismantles the only tools that existed. Both are now moot for licensed operators, and the self-exclusion register has no legal operator population to bind.

The implication for B2Tech is that Brazil's payments environment is now actively hostile and legally weaponised. Serving Brazilian customers from offshore would require routing around Pix controls that the Central Bank is being instructed to tighten, would expose any Brazilian payment partner to regulatory sanction, and would place the operator's brand and affiliates inside the Consumer Code, CDC counter-advertising and PF/Coaf perimeter. That is a risk profile incompatible with a licensed B2B/B2C group's compliance posture.

segments.name: Operator landscape, sponsorship fallout & exempt verticals
segments.headline: 84 licensees and 193 brands have been written to zero, Brazilian football has lost its dominant sponsor category, and only Caixa's lotteries remain untouched.
narrative: By H1-2026 the SPA had 84 authorised companies operating 193 brands, up from 77 companies and 159 brands a year earlier and 79 companies at December 2025. The SPA does not publish operator-level GGR or market shares, and the GR8_TECH report's ranking of the ten leading pre-ban brands sits behind a registration wall, so leader shares are n/a here; the groups commonly cited by traffic and sponsorship presence before the ban included Betano (Kaizen), bet365, Superbet, Betnacional (Flutter/NSX), Esportes da Sorte and Sportingbet (Entain) [names from prior knowledge, shares unverified]. Multi-homing was high — 27.8% of Q1-2026 bettors used four or more operators — which, combined with the bonus ban, points to a market competing on product and odds rather than acquisition spend.

Sunk capital is material. At R$30m (~$5.9m) per authorisation, the 84 licensees had paid on the order of R$2.5bn (~$0.49bn) in outorgas, all now forfeited without refund or indemnity under the MP, alongside Brazilian corporate structures, local payment integrations, SIGAP reporting stacks and marketing commitments. Deloitte's Malta practice has already issued guidance that the ban is an impairment-testing trigger for year-end reporting, and GR8_TECH notes that growth forecasts and sports-sponsorship budgets built on Brazil have been cut. The contested question in ADI 8.027 — whether acquired rights under a five-year authorisation can be extinguished by provisional measure — is the only route to recovery, and the rapporteur's remarks on 3 Nov were not encouraging.

Football is the most visible collateral damage. In 2025 every Série A club had a master sponsor and betting operators had become the central investors in Brazilian football, sponsoring large and small clubs and the main competitions. All advertising and sponsorship signage had to be removed by 5 Oct 2026; Latin Times estimates roughly US$200m of football sponsorship was wiped out, Flamengo told the STF that ~R$45m (~$8.8m) of its R$290m (~$57m) annual revenue was tied to betting sponsors and pitch-side advertising, and Flamengo, Botafogo, Fluminense, Grêmio, Cruzeiro and others publicly branded the measure 'the end of Brazilian football'. Clubs pressed Justice Fux for an injunction in early October and, at the hearing, asked for a gradual transition and legal security for contracts — which is the most likely locus of any Congressional amendment.

Outside the ban's perimeter, the picture is thin on data. Caixa Econômica Federal's federal lotteries (Mega-Sena and the rest) are expressly exempt as 'other lottery modalities'; their 2025–26 sales figures were not verified in this cycle (n/a). State and Federal District fixed-odds concessions — the Loterj-style regimes that were already territorially constrained by the STF in early 2025 — are swept into the prohibition. The long-running bill to legalise land-based casinos, bingo and jogo do bicho (PL 2.234/2022) had not been voted by the Senate plenary at last verification and has no realistic prospect in the current political climate [prior knowledge; unverified]. Pari-mutuel horse-race betting is governed by separate legislation and is not referenced in the MP summaries we read; treat its status as n/a.

For B2Tech the operator read-through is twofold. First, incumbents with Brazil-heavy portfolios are impaired and distracted, which marginally improves competitive conditions in the rest of LatAm where their capital will be redeployed. Second, if Brazil ever re-opens under a narrower regime, the field is reset: outorgas are gone, brands have been dark, and a fresh licensing round would favour entrants with clean capital and no legacy litigation — but the earliest such window is late 2027, and only if the committee rewrite scenario materialises.

highlights.text: Proven demand at scale: 30.4m bettors and a ~R$40bn (~$7.8bn) annualised GGR run-rate make Brazil the largest latent pool in LatAm; if a regime is rebuilt, day-one volume exists without market-making spend.

A compromise space is visible: the opposition and clubs distinguish sports betting from online casino, 99 amendments are on file, and the committee rewrite is where a narrower (sports-only, ad-restricted) regime could emerge in 2027–28.

Field reset: all outorgas are forfeited and brands dark, so any re-licensing round would not favour incumbents' sunk capital; a clean entrant with asset-light B2B exposure could compete on equal footing.

Regulatory plumbing already exists — SIGAP reporting, .bet.br domains, the centralised self-exclusion register, Pix KYC rails — so operational time-to-market on any re-opening would be months, not years.

Bonus-free, high-hold economics: implied hold rose to 22.9% in H1-2026 on a statutory sign-up-bonus ban, a template that would likely carry into any successor regime and favours product-led operators.

Capacity redeployment: impaired Brazil-heavy incumbents are pulling marketing and capital toward Argentina, Peru, Colombia and Mexico; Portuguese-language product can be redirected to Portugal and Lusophone Africa.

lowlights.text: Zero legal addressable market: every authorisation was extinguished on 25 Oct 2026 and sites have been offline since 6 Oct; there is no lawful way to serve Brazilian customers today.

Expropriation without compensation: ~R$2.5bn (~$0.49bn) of five-year outorgas were cancelled by provisional measure with no refund or indemnity — a precedent that must be priced into any future Brazilian licence.

Political alignment against the industry: a re-elected president publicly campaigning for the ban, an AGU and Health Ministry framing it as public health, and an STF rapporteur who said bets should be banned.
The fiscal argument has been discounted: the Treasury has booked R$5.15bn (~$1.01bn) of lost 2027 revenue in the MP itself, so tax-yield lobbying has little traction.

Payment rails weaponised: Pix rejection, bank/PSP prohibition, a BCB real-time return system and platform fines up to 10% of Brazil revenue make grey-market service of Brazil an AML/criminal exposure, not a commercial option.

Legal vacuum risk even on lapse: if the MP expires unconverted (~Jan/Feb 2027), licences do not revive; a new authorisation round under uncertain rules would be needed, and litigation over acquired rights could run for years.
Data opacity: the SPA has not published a 2026 Panorama; H1-2026 series disagree by ~1% and FY2025 by ~R$3.7bn; no sports/casino split or operator shares exist to size a sports-only successor market.

forecast.intro: The 'bridge' for Brazil is from a ~R$40bn (~$7.8bn) annualised regulated GGR run-rate (H1-2026: R$20.07–20.28bn) to zero from 6 Oct 2026, with the federal take moving from R$9.95bn (~$1.95bn) in 2025 to a government-booked loss of R$1.54bn in 2026 and R$5.15bn (~$1.01bn) in 2027. The moving parts are not market variables but institutional ones: whether the joint committee is installed and what its rapporteur writes before 23 Nov 2026 (or the ~Jan/Feb 2027 extension); whether Justice Fux rules on ADI 8.027 and in which direction after a hearing at which he voiced support for prohibition; and whether a re-elected Lula government, which issued the MP as a campaign measure, is willing to trade a transition for the clubs' sponsorship contracts.

forecast.view: Our independent view is that **prohibition holds through 2027 in the base case (we estimate ~55–60% probability)** — either by conversion with amendments (transition relief for club contracts, refund and enforcement tweaks) or by a lapse followed by a replacement bill, since the Executive has already absorbed the fiscal cost and the STF rapporteur has signalled sympathy. The main alternative (**~30%**) is a committee rewrite that re-creates a **narrower regulated regime from 2027–28: sports betting only, online casino prohibited, advertising and sponsorship tightly capped, deposit limits and welfare-fund blocks retained, and a fresh licensing round** — plausible because the opposition and clubs have framed the debate as casino-versus-sports and because 99 amendments exist to carry it. Judicial suspension is the tail (**~10–15%**). If a sports-only market re-opened, we would size it at **R$12–18bn (~$2.4–3.5bn) of annual GGR [analyst estimate]**, on the assumption that casino was more than half of 2025–26 GGR (not published; inferred from rising hold and survey mix), with higher hold and lower marketing intensity than the 2025 market. **Revenue direction for any Brazil-exposed operator: zero in 2027 base case; margin/leverage: impairments of licences and intangibles in FY2026 accounts, with outorga recovery dependent on ADI 8.027.** For B2Tech: no entry; keep a compliance-grade monitoring file; reassess only on committee installation with a rapporteur text that preserves a licensed sportsbook.
watch: Installation of the MP 1.394 joint committee, identity of the rapporteur, and whether the committee text preserves any licensed activity (sports-only) or merely softens wind-down terms — before 23 Nov 2026 or the ~Jan/Feb 2027 extension.
Any ruling by Justice Fux on ADI 8.027 (ANJL) — injunction, denial, or referral to the full bench — and whether the Court addresses acquired rights to the R$30m outorgas.
Whether the MP lapses unconverted; if so, the form of the Congressional legislative decree governing acts taken while it was in force and any new government bill or MP.

Central Bank implementation of the mandated Pix rejection/return system and its targeting of intermediated-Pix gateways and crypto on-ramps used by offshore sites; enforcement actions against payment intermediaries.
Monthly blocking statistics from the Interinstitutional Committee / Anatel (16,627 sites in the first two weeks) and first platform fines under the 10%-of-revenue regime.
Publication by the SPA of final 2026 SIGAP data (Jan–Sep) to reconcile the FY2025 (R$36.96bn vs R$40.69bn) and H1-2026 (R$20.07bn vs R$20.28bn) discrepancies and, ideally, a sports/casino GGR split.
Club-sponsorship settlements and whether Congress inserts a contract-transition clause; CBF/Série A commercial revenue disclosures for 2026–27.
Listed-operator FY2026 disclosures (impairments, Brazil revenue exposure) and any announced exits or re-entry conditions.
